nodes.label: [B]/[C]/[S] Dialect-Tag Convention
nodes.rationale: Alexander & Elias-Bursać's own textbook explicitly frames its [B]/[C]/[S] tagging as a simplification of a frequency gradient rather than a hard categorical split among the three national standards; this is treated as load-bearing for interpreting every Usage Tier/Attested Region tag drawn from this book.
nodes.community_name: B/C/S Tagging & the STRUKE Professions Table

nodes.label: Ekavian/Ijekavian (jat-reflex) Pronunciation Split
nodes.rationale: Cuts across the B/C/S national-standard split rather than mapping one-to-one onto it: Croatian and Bosnian use only ijekavian, while Serbian speakers split geographically (ekavian in most of Serbia proper, ijekavian in Bosnia, southwestern Serbia, and Montenegro).
nodes.community_name: B/C/S Tagging & the STRUKE Professions Table

nodes.label: da li / li Yes-No Question Marker Placement
nodes.rationale: Serbian's most frequent pattern places da li before the verb; Bosnian and Croatian's most frequent pattern places li after the verb — both produce an identical question, a syntactic (word-order) rather than lexical B/C/S divergence, confirmed independently across multiple lessons and both the Alexander/Elias-Bursać and Magner textbooks.
nodes.community_name: B/C/S Tagging & the STRUKE Professions Table
nodes.norm_label: da li / li yes-no question marker placement

nodes.label: B/C/S Vocabulary Markedness — Coexisting vs. Opposing Synonyms
nodes.rationale: The source flags that a [C]/[S]-style tag does not always signal a strict binary split: some tagged words simply coexist alongside a pan-regional [B,C,S] synonym rather than opposing it one-to-one (e.g. abecèda [B,C,S] vs. regionally narrower àzbuka [S]; paradajz [B,C,S] vs. rajčica [C]). Bosnian usage varies per word, sometimes preferring the Serbian term, sometimes the Croatian term, sometimes having its own distinct word.

nodes.label: Genitive Case: Formation and Core Uses
nodes.rationale: One of the most important BCS cases: masculine/neuter Gsg endings equal the animate accusative; feminine nouns take -e or -i. Governs prepositions like iz, kod, od, do; required after nema; expresses partitive sense (žèliš li sòka? 'would you like some juice?') vs. accusative for the whole/general idea; possessive pronominal adjectives keep short-form Gsg endings, an explicit B/C/S register split (short required in Croatian, long more frequent in Bosnian/Serbian).
nodes.norm_label: genitive case: formation and core uses

nodes.label: 16 BCS Verb Conjugation Types
nodes.rationale: BCS verbs are grouped into 16 conjugation types by the relationship between the infinitive and present-tense stem: type 1 is a-conjugation, types 2-4 are i-conjugation, all remaining types are e-conjugation. Identical-looking infinitives can belong to different types (dòvesti 1sg dovèdem = type 13 vs. dòvesti 1sg dovèzem = type 14), so infinitive and present tense must be memorized together.

nodes.label: Consonant-Softening Comparative Adjective Pattern
nodes.rationale: A productive comparative pattern replaces the adjective's stem-final consonant with its softened phonological counterpart (k→č, g→ž, h→š, t→ć, d→đ, p→plj, b→blj, v→vlj, m→mlj) rather than adding a suffix; the same softening set recurs in passive-participle formation and the feminine instrumental singular, marking it as a systemic BCS morphophonological process rather than an isolated rule.

nodes.label: Passive Participle Formation (-n/-t/-en markers)
nodes.rationale: Passive participles are formed by adding -n, -t, or -en to either the infinitive stem or the present stem, then regular adjectival endings; -en is the most complex, sometimes requiring the same consonant-softening set used elsewhere in the grammar for comparative adjectives, verbal nouns, and the feminine instrumental singular — a recurring cross-cutting phonological pattern in BCS morphology.

nodes.label: Subjectless Sentences (dative/genitive/accusative logical subjects)
nodes.rationale: Subjectless sentences lack a grammatical subject entirely, or carry a 'logical subject' in a non-nominative case: dative subjectless sentences include inclinational se-verbs (sviđati se); genitive expresses measurement/quantity; accusative identifies the experiencer of an emotion like fear (strah me je 'I am afraid'), with the preposition od obligatory in Serbian but optional in Bosnian/Croatian.

nodes.label: Bošnjak/Bošnjakinja vs. Bosanac/Bosanka Ethnonym-Demonym Distinction
nodes.rationale: A sociolinguistically significant distinction the source flags explicitly: Bošnjak/Bošnjakinja ('Bosniak') refers specifically to members of Bosnia and Herzegovina's Muslim community, while Bosanac/Bosanka ('Bosnian') is the civic/residency term covering any resident of Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of ethnicity or religion.

nodes.label: Future Tense (compound, ću/ćeš/će auxiliary)
nodes.rationale: The future is a compound tense: infinitive (or da + present) plus a clitic auxiliary derived from hteti/htjeti 'to want'. Orthographic split: Croatian writes the infinitive+clitic separately (ùčit ću), Serbian fuses them (ùčiću); Bosnian permits both spelling conventions for -sti infinitives.

nodes.label: da + present vs. infinitive (Croatian/Serbian/Bosnian frequency split)
nodes.rationale: Croatian almost always uses an infinitive after a verb like 'want' (želimo učiti), Serbian usually prefers da + present (želimo da učimo), and Bosnian uses both about equally; when the two verbs have different subjects, only da + present is grammatical. This is a genuine relative-frequency/register distinction rather than a strict grammaticality difference, confirmed again in Lesson 5's parallel-dialogue evidence and explicitly discussed as a named 'Note' by the source.

nodes.label: Bosnian Turkish-Derived Kinship Terms (Islamic Heritage Vocabulary)
nodes.rationale: Bosnian retains a set of Turkish-derived words reflecting its Islamic cultural heritage, most visibly in family-relation terms: 'mother's brother' is ujak in S/C but dàidža in B; 'father's brother' is stric in S/C but àmidža in B; 'grandmother' is baba/baka in S/C but nèna in B. This is a productive B-vs-S/C lexical split distinct from the E/J pronunciation split and from the general [B]/[C]/[S] tagging convention.
nodes.norm_label: bosnian turkish-derived kinship terms (islamic heritage vocabulary)

nodes.label: Regional Discourse Particles (bre, bona/bolan, je li?/jel'?)
nodes.rationale: Bosnian speakers use bòna/bolan (from bolan 'painful') as a term of address comparable to colloquial American English 'man'; Serbian speakers add bre for emphasis, comparable to filler 'you know'/'like'; some Croatian and Bosnian speakers use the interrogative tag je li? or its contractions jel'?/jel'da?/jel'te?.

nodes.label: Montenegrin Not Treated as a Fourth Standard-Language Tag
nodes.rationale: The source explicitly declines to add an [M] (Montenegrin) tag alongside [B]/[C]/[S]: Montenegro's 2006 independence and 2007 constitution named 'Montenegrin' the official language and set up a 2008 codification council, but the codification process was too recent and unvalidated by the speech community to treat as a fourth standard on par with B/C/S at the time of writing — unlike B/C/S, whose separateness the source partly ties to distinct religious/cultural histories, Montenegro is described as sharing that history with Serbia. Later found to be substantially deepened/confirmed by the Grammar: Sociolinguistic Commentary volume's Ch. 25 (Nikčević 1997 proposals), per the extraction checklist.

nodes.label: "Amusing Slang Usage" Source Annotation
nodes.rationale: The source itself explicitly labels this as slang: there is no grammatical affirmative counterpart to nèmoj, but B, C, and S colloquial usage has produced the ungrammatical-yet-popular retort 'Ma moj!'/'Ma da moj!' in response to 'Ma nèmoj!' — paralleling English 'No way!' → 'Way!'. This is the project's first source-self-labeled slang instance.
